title: Genomics and Proteomics
tagline: Read whole genomes, measure whole proteomes, and learn how to turn billions of data points into biology.
overview: This course follows the arc from sequencing a genome to measuring its products. It covers genome organisation and the Human Genome Project, sequencing technologies, assembly and annotation, variation and GWAS, transcriptomics, functional genomics and epigenomics, metagenomics and comparative genomics, mass-spectrometry proteomics, and quantitative proteomics with interactomics. The units follow the standard content of a BSc Honours genomics and proteomics course.
whyItMatters: Modern biology and medicine are data driven. Cancer genomics, rare-disease diagnosis, pathogen surveillance and biomarker discovery all depend on sequencing and proteomics, and the skills of reading these data critically transfer to any omics-based research project.
studyTips: Draw each workflow (sequencing, RNA-seq, bottom-up MS) as a flowchart from sample to figure, then say what could go wrong at each step.
Open real datasets in the Ensembl, UCSC and Human Protein Atlas browsers while you study; concepts stick when you see them on actual genes.
Learn to read the plots (Manhattan, volcano, UMAP, mass spectra) before you learn the maths behind them.
Keep a glossary of file formats (FASTQ, BAM, VCF, mzML) and what each one stores.

units.title: Genome Organisation and the Human Genome Project
units.hook: In 1990 a few hundred scientists set out to read three billion letters of human DNA, and the first draft landed in 2001 as two rival papers published a few days apart. It took until 2022 for someone to read the whole thing end to end with no gaps. Before you can study genomes, you need a feel for what one actually looks like: mostly not genes, and mostly repetitive.
learningObjectives: Define genome, chromosome, gene, exon, intron and intergenic region, and say roughly what fraction of the human genome each occupies.
Explain why genome size (the C-value) does not track organismal complexity.
Compare the architecture of prokaryotic, organellar and eukaryotic genomes.
Describe the two strategies used to sequence the human genome (hierarchical clone-by-clone vs whole-genome shotgun).
Classify the main repeat families (transposable elements, tandem repeats, segmental duplications) and say why they made assembly hard.
Say what the telomere-to-telomere (T2T) assembly added to earlier reference genomes.

keyConcepts.definition: The complete set of DNA in a cell or organism, including nuclear chromosomes, organelle genomes and any plasmids.
Genome size varies enormously between species (some amphibians and plants have genomes many times larger than ours) without matching organismal complexity; the extra DNA is mostly repeats.
In humans only about 1 to 2 percent of the genome encodes protein; roughly 20,000 protein-coding genes are annotated.
A mobile DNA sequence (for example Alu and LINE-1 in humans) that copies or moves itself; together such elements derive roughly half of the human genome.
Short sequence units repeated head to tail, such as microsatellites, minisatellites and the alpha-satellite DNA of centromeres.
A large (over 1 kb) block of near-identical DNA copied to another place in the genome; a hotspot for rearrangement and a headache for assemblers.
Clone large fragments (BACs), map them, then sequence each clone by shotgun; the public Human Genome Project approach.
Shear the whole genome, sequence the pieces at random and assemble them computationally; the approach used by Celera and now standard.
A gap-free, telomere-to-telomere human reference (CHM13) completed in 2022 using long reads, which added about 200 Mb of previously unresolved sequence.

deeper.beginner: Think of the genome as a library in which only a few shelves hold instruction manuals (genes). Much of the rest is regulatory notes, copies of the same page printed thousands of times (repeats), and sections whose purpose we are still working out. The Human Genome Project made the first draft catalogue of that library. Analogy break: a library has an index; the genome does not, which is why annotation is a whole discipline.
deeper.intermediate: Human nuclear DNA is about 3.1 Gb in 23 chromosome pairs, with a 16.6 kb circular mitochondrial genome that is inherited maternally and carries 13 protein-coding genes. Bacterial genomes are compact (a few Mb, gene-dense, often a single circular chromosome with operons), whereas eukaryotic genomes carry introns, long intergenic stretches and abundant repeats. The initial human drafts were released in 2001; the finished euchromatic sequence followed in 2003, but centromeres, acrocentric short arms and large segmental duplications stayed unresolved until long-read assemblies.
deeper.advanced: Short reads cannot span repeats longer than the read length, so near-identical copies collapse in the assembly or leave gaps. The T2T-CHM13 project used a haploid hydatidiform mole cell line (so there is one allele per locus), combined PacBio HiFi and Oxford Nanopore ultra-long reads, and resolved the centromeric satellite arrays and rDNA arrays. A single reference also biases analysis towards one ancestry, which is why pangenome references that represent many people are replacing the single-genome model.

commonMistakes: Equating genome size with gene number: a bigger genome mostly means more repeats, not more genes.
Saying 'junk DNA' means useless: a lot of non-coding DNA is regulatory, structural (centromeres, telomeres) or produces functional RNAs, and the fraction that is truly dispensable is still debated.
Thinking the 2001 draft was complete; it had thousands of gaps and the first gap-free human genome only appeared in 2022.

units.title: DNA Sequencing Technologies: Sanger to Long Reads
units.hook: The first human genome cost around three billion dollars and a decade. Today a genome can be sequenced in a day for a few hundred dollars, and a pocket-sized device can read DNA in a hospital ward or a rainforest. The leaps came from changing the chemistry, not the goal.
learningObjectives: Explain chain-termination (Sanger) sequencing and why it is still used for validation.
Describe Illumina sequencing by synthesis: library prep, bridge amplification, reversible terminators and imaging.
Explain how nanopore and PacBio HiFi sequencing read single molecules and what error profile each has.
Compare short- and long-read technologies for read length, accuracy, throughput and cost.
Interpret FASTQ files, Phred quality scores and read depth (coverage).
Choose a sequencing strategy for a given biological question (variant calling, de novo assembly, RNA-seq, structural variants).

keyConcepts.definition: Sanger method: dideoxynucleotides (ddNTPs) lack a 3'-OH, so extension stops when one is incorporated, producing fragments that end at every position.
Illumina chemistry: fluorescent reversible-terminator nucleotides are added one cycle at a time to clusters of identical DNA molecules and imaged.
Fragmenting DNA, repairing ends and ligating adapters so fragments can bind a flow cell, be amplified and be primed for sequencing.
Q = -10 log10(P error). Q20 means a 1 percent chance the base is wrong; Q30 means 0.1 percent.
The average number of reads covering each base; 30x is common for human whole-genome resequencing.
A DNA strand is threaded through a protein pore and changes in ionic current identify the bases passing through; reads can be extremely long.
Circular consensus sequencing: a single molecule is read repeatedly in zero-mode waveguides to give reads of about 15-20 kb with accuracy above 99.9 percent.
A text format storing each read's sequence and per-base quality string.

deeper.beginner: A sequencer does not read a genome from start to finish. It reads millions of short snippets and software reassembles them. Short reads are cheap and accurate but ambiguous in repeats; long reads span repeats but each base is read with more noise (nanopore) or at higher cost (HiFi). Sanger sequencing reads one fragment at a time and is the gold standard for confirming a single variant.
deeper.intermediate: Illumina reads (typically 75-300 bp, paired-end) have substitution errors at roughly 0.1 percent and enormous throughput, making them the workhorse for resequencing, RNA-seq and ChIP-seq. Nanopore reads can exceed 100 kb and can detect base modifications such as 5-methylcytosine directly from the signal; error rates have fallen steadily with new pores and basecallers. Read QC (FastQC, adapter trimming) comes before any analysis because contamination or quality drop-off biases everything downstream.
deeper.advanced: Short-read PCR amplification introduces GC bias and duplicate reads; PCR-free libraries reduce this. Long-read platforms enable phased haplotypes, structural variant calling and complete assemblies, and direct RNA sequencing removes reverse-transcription artefacts. Error models differ (indels in homopolymers for nanopore, random errors for HiFi), so variant callers and assemblers are platform-specific, and hybrid strategies often combine accurate short reads with long scaffolding reads.

commonMistakes: Assuming a higher Phred score means more reads: it is a per-base error probability.
Thinking long reads are always better: for SNP calling at scale, accurate short reads are cheaper.
Ignoring that 30x coverage is an average; some regions (GC-extreme, repetitive) are covered far less.

selfCheck.question: In Sanger sequencing, chain termination occurs because ddNTPs
options: Lack a 3'-OH group needed for the next phosphodiester bond
selfCheck.explanation: Without a 3'-OH, DNA polymerase cannot add the next nucleotide, so each ddNTP stops the chain at a specific base.

selfCheck.question: A base with Phred score Q30 has an error probability of about
selfCheck.explanation: Q = -10 log10(P) so Q30 means P = 10^-3, or 0.1 percent.

options: It always has lower per-base error
It can span repeats and resolve structural variants

selfCheck.explanation: Long reads cross repeated regions that short reads cannot place uniquely.

units.title: Genome Assembly and Annotation
units.hook: A sequencer hands you billions of tiny fragments with no addresses. Putting them back together is a jigsaw where thousands of pieces are identical blue sky, and then you still have to write the captions: which stretches are genes, and what do they do?
learningObjectives: Explain the overlap-layout-consensus and de Bruijn graph approaches to assembly and when each is used.
Interpret assembly quality metrics such as N50, contig count and BUSCO completeness.
Differentiate reference-guided mapping from de novo assembly.
Describe how scaffolding with long reads, Hi-C or optical maps orders and orients contigs.
Distinguish structural from functional annotation and explain ab initio, evidence-based and homology-based gene prediction.
Use a genome browser to inspect gene models and supporting evidence.

keyConcepts.definition: A contiguous stretch of sequence assembled from overlapping reads with no gaps.
Contigs ordered and oriented with estimated gap sizes using paired-end, long-range or Hi-C information.
Reads are cut into k-mers; nodes are (k-1)-mers and edges are k-mers, and an assembly is a path through the graph; efficient for huge numbers of short reads.
Find pairwise overlaps between reads, lay them out, then call a consensus; suited to long reads.
The contig length such that contigs of that length or longer contain half of the total assembled bases; a measure of contiguity, not correctness.
A score of how many expected single-copy conserved genes for a lineage are found complete in an assembly; a proxy for completeness.
Using statistical models (for example hidden Markov models) to find signals such as start codons, splice sites and codon usage without external evidence.
Structural annotation locates genes and features; functional annotation assigns names, domains, GO terms and pathways to them.
Aligning reads to an existing genome instead of assembling from scratch; far cheaper but blind to sequence the reference lacks.

deeper.beginner: De novo assembly is like reassembling many copies of a shredded book: you look for passages that overlap and chain them. Repeated paragraphs (genomic repeats) confuse this. Annotation then marks up the finished book: where chapters (genes) begin and end, and what they are about. Analogy break: a book has one correct text, whereas a population has many valid genome sequences.
deeper.intermediate: Short-read assemblers (SPAdes, MEGAHIT) use de Bruijn graphs, while long-read assemblers (Flye, hifiasm) use overlap-based methods. A good assembly has a high N50, few misassemblies and high BUSCO completeness, but N50 can be inflated by mistaken joins, so it should be read alongside the other metrics. Eukaryotic gene prediction combines ab initio tools (AUGUSTUS), RNA-seq alignments and protein homology, then manual curation for important genes; pipelines such as Ensembl and NCBI RefSeq publish the standard annotations.
deeper.advanced: Repeats and heterozygosity create bubbles and branches in the graph; haplotype-resolved assemblers use HiFi reads and trio or Hi-C data to separate maternal and paternal haplotypes. Choosing k involves a trade-off: small k connects through low coverage but collapses repeats, large k resolves repeats but fragments at low coverage, so multiple k values are often used. Annotation accuracy depends on expression evidence: genes not expressed in your RNA-seq samples are often missed or mispredicted.

commonMistakes: Treating a high N50 as proof of a good assembly; it ignores correctness and completeness.
Believing a predicted gene is real without supporting transcript or protein evidence.
Assuming mapping to a reference finds all variation; sequence absent from the reference is invisible.

units.title: Human Genetic Variation and GWAS
units.hook: Any two people differ at roughly one position in a thousand, and every one of those spots is a small clue about ancestry, disease risk or drug response. Genome-wide association studies turned that variation into a map of where in the genome common diseases begin.
learningObjectives: Differentiate SNPs, indels, copy-number variants and structural variants.
Describe a variant-calling workflow from reads to a VCF file.
Explain linkage disequilibrium and why a GWAS hit is rarely the causal variant.
Interpret a Manhattan plot, a QQ plot and the genome-wide significance threshold of 5 x 10^-8.
Discuss polygenic scores and the bias that arises from ancestry-skewed cohorts.
Use population databases (1000 Genomes, gnomAD) to judge whether a variant is rare.

keyConcepts.definition: A single-nucleotide polymorphism: a position where two or more bases are common in a population.
A rearrangement larger than about 50 bp: deletions, duplications, insertions, inversions and translocations.
Variant Call Format: a text file listing variant positions, alleles and genotype calls per sample.
Non-random association between alleles at nearby loci because they are inherited together in haplotype blocks.
A study testing hundreds of thousands to millions of variants across many individuals for association with a trait.
A p-value threshold of 5 x 10^-8, which accounts for about a million independent tests.
How common an allele is in a population; rare variants tend to have larger effects and common variants small ones.
A weighted sum of many risk alleles used to estimate a person's genetic liability to a trait.
Statistical and functional analysis to pick out the likely causal variant inside an associated LD block.

deeper.beginner: Imagine comparing the spelling of one sentence across thousands of people. If people with a disease tend to spell a word one way, that word is flagged, but the flagged word may simply sit next to the real culprit because they are always copied together. A GWAS gives you a neighbourhood, not a street address.
deeper.intermediate: Variant calling aligns reads to the reference, marks duplicates, recalibrates, then calls differences (for example GATK or DeepVariant). A GWAS then uses regression of the trait on genotype with covariates (age, sex, principal components for ancestry), tested at each SNP. The Manhattan plot shows -log10 p by position; a QQ plot checks whether inflation suggests population stratification. The 1000 Genomes Project (2,504 individuals from 26 populations) provided the LD and frequency reference used for imputation.
deeper.advanced: Most GWAS signals are non-coding and enriched in regulatory elements, so linking them to genes needs eQTL colocalisation, chromatin conformation or CRISPR perturbation. Heritability is spread over thousands of variants of tiny effect (polygenicity), and the proportion captured by significant SNPs is only part of the total; rare variants and structural variants account for some of the rest. Polygenic scores trained mostly in European-ancestry cohorts transfer poorly to other ancestries, a scientific and an equity problem.

commonMistakes: Calling the lead GWAS SNP 'the causal variant' without fine mapping.
Interpreting an association as causation or as individual-level prediction.
Ignoring population stratification, which can create false positives.

selfCheck.question: Why is the standard GWAS significance threshold 5 x 10^-8?
options: It corrects for roughly a million independent common-variant tests
It is the lowest number a computer can store
It is chosen separately for each disease
selfCheck.explanation: With about a million independent tests, 0.05 divided by a million is approximately 5 x 10^-8.

selfCheck.question: A GWAS lead SNP is usually not the causal variant because of
selfCheck.explanation: Variants inherited together in a haplotype all show association; fine mapping is required to find the causal one.

units.title: Transcriptomics: Microarrays, RNA-seq and Single Cells
units.hook: Every cell in your body has the same genome but reads it differently. A neuron and a hepatocyte differ because of which genes are being transcribed, and the transcriptome is the readout of that decision at one moment in time.
learningObjectives: Contrast microarrays with RNA-seq in terms of dynamic range, novelty detection and cost.
Outline an RNA-seq workflow: RNA extraction, library prep (poly-A selection vs rRNA depletion), sequencing, alignment, counting.
Explain why raw counts must be normalised and name common units (CPM, TPM) and models (negative binomial).
Describe differential expression analysis, multiple-testing correction and what a volcano plot shows.
Explain how droplet single-cell RNA-seq uses cell barcodes and UMIs, and what clustering reveals.
State the main limitations of bulk and single-cell transcriptomics.

keyConcepts.definition: The complete set of RNA transcripts present in a cell or tissue under defined conditions.
A chip carrying thousands of fixed DNA probes; labelled cDNA hybridises and fluorescence intensity reports abundance of known sequences.
Sequencing of cDNA made from RNA, giving digital counts of reads per transcript and the ability to discover novel transcripts and isoforms.
Two ways of removing the 80-90 percent of RNA that is ribosomal: capturing polyadenylated mRNA or removing rRNA to keep non-polyadenylated species.
Transcripts per million: read counts normalised for gene length and sequencing depth so values are comparable between genes in a sample.
Statistical testing for genes whose expression differs between conditions, usually with count-based models (DESeq2, edgeR) and false discovery rate control.
Unique molecular identifier: a random barcode added before amplification so duplicate reads can be collapsed to one original molecule.
Profiling the transcriptome of thousands of individual cells, usually by isolating each cell in a droplet with a barcoded bead.
Technical variation between runs or days that can mimic or hide biological differences if not controlled in design and analysis.

deeper.beginner: A microarray asks, for genes you already know about, how bright is each spot. RNA-seq counts molecules directly and can discover transcripts you did not know existed. Single-cell RNA-seq goes one step further by asking what each individual cell is doing, which matters because a tissue average can hide rare cell types entirely.
deeper.intermediate: Reads are aligned with splice-aware aligners (STAR, HISAT2) or pseudo-aligned (Salmon, kallisto) and assigned to genes. Counts depend on library size and gene length, so comparisons use normalisation (size factors in DESeq2, TMM in edgeR). Thousands of genes are tested, so p-values are adjusted (Benjamini-Hochberg FDR). In single-cell data, cell barcodes identify the droplet, UMIs correct amplification bias, and dimensionality reduction (PCA, UMAP) plus clustering reveals cell types.
deeper.advanced: Bulk RNA-seq counts are modelled with the negative binomial because variance exceeds the mean (overdispersion). Single-cell data are sparse because of low capture efficiency, which is partly technical dropout and partly biology, so methods model zero inflation or use ambient-RNA correction. Replicates are essential: pseudo-replication across cells within a single donor inflates significance. Spatial transcriptomics and multi-ome assays are extending this to tissue location and chromatin state.

commonMistakes: Using FPKM or TPM values for statistical testing instead of raw counts with a count model.
Skipping biological replicates and treating cells as independent samples.
Reading UMAP distances literally: cluster shapes and gaps in the plot are not quantitative.

options: To count original molecules by collapsing PCR duplicates
selfCheck.explanation: UMIs are added before amplification so reads sharing the same UMI and gene are counted as one molecule.

selfCheck.question: Why is multiple-testing correction needed in differential expression?
options: Thousands of genes are tested at once, producing many false positives by chance
selfCheck.explanation: At p < 0.05 about 5 percent of non-changing genes would appear significant; FDR control limits this.

units.title: Functional Genomics and Epigenomics
units.hook: Knowing the sequence is like owning a dictionary without knowing which words are used where. Functional genomics asks which parts of the sequence are active, which are switched off, and what happens if you break them.
learningObjectives: Explain what ENCODE and Roadmap Epigenomics set out to map and summarise the debate about 'percent functional'.
Describe ChIP-seq and ATAC-seq and what each tells you about regulation.
Explain how bisulfite sequencing detects DNA methylation.
Describe Hi-C and how three-dimensional genome organisation links enhancers to genes.
Explain pooled CRISPR knockout, CRISPRi and CRISPRa screens and how hits are scored.
Choose an assay to answer a given regulatory question.

keyConcepts.definition: The collection of chemical modifications and chromatin states (DNA methylation, histone marks, accessibility) that regulate gene activity without changing the DNA sequence.
Chromatin immunoprecipitation followed by sequencing: antibodies pull down DNA bound by a protein or histone mark, and reads map to where it sits.
Uses the Tn5 transposase to insert adapters preferentially into open chromatin, mapping accessible regulatory regions.
Treating DNA with bisulfite converts unmethylated cytosine to uracil (read as T) while 5-methylcytosine is protected, revealing methylation by comparison with the reference.
A distal regulatory element that increases transcription of a target gene, often marked by H3K27ac and accessible chromatin.
A proximity-ligation method that captures which genomic regions contact each other in 3D, revealing loops and topologically associating domains.
A pooled library of guide RNAs perturbs thousands of genes at once; guide abundance before and after selection shows which genes affect a phenotype.
A variant associated with expression level of a gene; a bridge between GWAS signals and gene regulation.
Statistical identification of regions with more mapped reads than background in ChIP-seq or ATAC-seq.

deeper.beginner: Each cell type switches on a different set of regulatory regions, and chemical tags on DNA and histones help decide which ones are open. Functional genomics assays photograph that state, and CRISPR screens test it by disabling genes one at a time. ENCODE's headline was that most of the genome shows some biochemical activity, but whether biochemical activity equals biological function is still argued.
deeper.intermediate: ChIP-seq needs a good antibody and an input control; ATAC-seq needs far fewer cells and no antibody. Histone marks have rules of thumb: H3K4me3 at active promoters, H3K27ac at active enhancers and promoters, H3K27me3 for Polycomb repression, H3K9me3 for heterochromatin. Hi-C shows that enhancers often act over tens to hundreds of kb by looping. In a CRISPR knockout screen, essential genes drop out of the population over time, and tools such as MAGeCK rank genes by guide depletion.
deeper.advanced: Bisulfite damage fragments DNA and cannot distinguish 5mC from 5hmC, whereas enzymatic (EM-seq) and nanopore methods preserve DNA or read modifications directly. ENCODE's 80 percent figure used a broad definition of 'biochemical event'; evolutionary conservation suggests that a smaller fraction, perhaps up to roughly 10 percent, is under selection, so definitions of function matter. CRISPRi/a screens (dCas9 fused to KRAB or activators) perturb regulatory elements without cutting DNA, so non-coding enhancers can be tested at scale.

commonMistakes: Equating a ChIP-seq peak with a functional regulatory element without perturbation evidence.
Forgetting that bisulfite conversion does not tell 5mC from 5hmC.
Assuming a CRISPR knockout always gives a complete loss of function (in-frame edits, copy number and gene redundancy confound results).

units.title: Metagenomics and Comparative Genomics
units.hook: A spoonful of soil or a drop of seawater holds thousands of microbial species, and the vast majority will never grow in a Petri dish. Metagenomics lets us sequence the community directly, and comparative genomics lets us read what evolution has kept and discarded across species.
learningObjectives: Differentiate 16S amplicon sequencing from shotgun metagenomics and say what each can and cannot tell you.
Describe a metagenomic workflow, including assembly, binning and metagenome-assembled genomes.
Interpret alpha and beta diversity measures at an introductory level.
Define core genome, accessory genome and pangenome.
Use synteny and orthology to compare genomes and infer conserved function.
Explain how comparative genomics identifies conserved non-coding elements and lineage-specific genes.

keyConcepts.definition: The collective genomes of all organisms in an environmental sample, sequenced without culturing.
Amplifying and sequencing hypervariable regions of the 16S ribosomal RNA gene to identify bacteria and archaea; cheap, but gives taxonomy and not function.
Sequencing all DNA in a sample; allows species- or strain-level profiling and functional gene content.
A metagenome-assembled genome: a draft genome reconstructed by binning contigs from a metagenomic assembly.
Alpha is diversity within a sample (richness, evenness); beta is how much composition differs between samples.
All genes found across a species, divided into the core genome (in every strain) and the accessory genome (in some).
Conserved order of genes along chromosomes between species.
Orthologs arise by speciation, paralogs by duplication within a lineage.
A non-coding sequence retained across species far more than expected by chance, suggesting a regulatory role.

deeper.beginner: Metagenomics asks who is there and what can they do, by sequencing everything without growing it. Comparative genomics lines up genomes and asks what changed. Regions that stay the same across hundreds of millions of years of evolution are probably doing something important, even if we do not yet know what.
deeper.intermediate: 16S profiling clusters reads into ASVs or OTUs and assigns taxonomy by database matching, but resolution is typically at genus level and copy number of 16S varies. Shotgun data allow gene-level and pathway-level profiling and strain tracking. Binning uses coverage and composition (tetranucleotide frequency) to group contigs; MAGs are assessed with tools like CheckM for completeness and contamination. For comparative work, orthologs are inferred by tools such as OrthoFinder and genome alignments reveal synteny breaks from rearrangements.
deeper.advanced: Compositional data are a trap: relative abundances sum to one, so an increase in one taxon forces apparent decreases in others, and methods that respect compositionality (CLR transforms, ANCOM) are preferred. Horizontal gene transfer shapes bacterial pangenomes, which are often open, meaning new genes keep appearing with each new strain sequenced. In vertebrates, ultraconserved elements and cross-species alignments (phastCons, phyloP) are used to prioritise non-coding variants from GWAS and clinical sequencing.

commonMistakes: Treating 16S relative abundance as absolute cell counts.
Assuming a MAG represents a single clean genome without checking contamination and completeness.
Mixing up orthologs (speciation) and paralogs (duplication) when transferring annotation.

units.title: Proteomics I: Separation and Mass Spectrometry
units.hook: The genome is the script, but proteins are the actors, and one gene can yield many different proteoforms through splicing and chemical modification. Proteomics identifies and counts those actors, and mass spectrometry is the tool that made it possible.
learningObjectives: Explain why the proteome is more complex and dynamic than the genome.
Describe protein and peptide separation by 2D gel electrophoresis and liquid chromatography.
Explain ionisation by ESI and MALDI and the principle of mass analysers (TOF, Orbitrap, quadrupole).
Outline a bottom-up proteomics workflow from sample to peptide-spectrum matches.
Contrast data-dependent (DDA) and data-independent (DIA) acquisition.
Explain how false discovery rate is controlled with a target-decoy database.

keyConcepts.definition: All proteins expressed by a cell, tissue or organism at a given time, including isoforms and modifications.
A specific molecular form of a protein, defined by its sequence variant, splice isoform and post-translational modifications.
Proteins are digested (usually with trypsin) into peptides that are analysed by LC-MS/MS and used to infer the proteins.
A protease that cleaves after lysine and arginine (except when followed by proline), giving peptides of a convenient size and charge for MS.
Soft ionisation methods that turn peptides or proteins into gas-phase ions without breaking them; electrospray (ESI) is coupled to liquid chromatography, MALDI uses a laser on a matrix.
A selected peptide ion is fragmented and the fragment masses form a pattern that reveals its amino acid sequence.
A scored assignment of an observed MS/MS spectrum to a peptide sequence in a database.
Searching spectra against real (target) and reversed or shuffled (decoy) sequences to estimate how many matches are false.
Data-independent acquisition: all precursors in broad m/z windows are fragmented, giving more complete and reproducible data at the cost of complex spectra.

deeper.beginner: A mass spectrometer is a very precise scale for molecules. You chop proteins into peptides, weigh them, break them in a controlled way and weigh the pieces; the pattern of piece masses spells the sequence. Software then matches those patterns to a database to say which protein each peptide came from.
deeper.intermediate: 2D gel electrophoresis separates proteins by isoelectric point and then size, and was the early workhorse, but modern proteomics usually digests the whole mixture and separates peptides by reverse-phase LC before ESI. High-resolution instruments such as the Orbitrap or time-of-flight analysers measure m/z with parts-per-million accuracy. Search engines (Mascot, MaxQuant, MSFragger) match spectra to predicted fragment ions; a 1 percent FDR at peptide and protein level is conventional.
deeper.advanced: The proteome has a huge dynamic range (in plasma about ten orders of magnitude between the most and least abundant proteins), so depletion, fractionation or faster instruments are needed to see low-abundance proteins. In bottom-up work the protein inference problem arises because shared peptides may map to multiple proteins. Top-down proteomics analyses intact proteins to preserve proteoform information but is harder for large proteins. Machine-learned predictors of retention time and fragment intensity now improve identification, particularly in DIA.

commonMistakes: Assuming one gene equals one protein; splicing and modification create many proteoforms.
Believing that no peptide detected means the protein is absent: it may be below the detection limit.
Ignoring false discovery control: unfiltered search results contain many wrong matches.

units.title: Proteomics II: Quantitation, Modifications and Interactions
units.hook: Knowing which proteins are present is only half the story. A cell responds to a signal in minutes by adding phosphate groups to existing proteins, and proteins rarely work alone. Quantitative proteomics, PTM mapping and interactomics put numbers and wiring diagrams on the proteome, and multi-omics ties it all to the genome.
learningObjectives: Compare label-free, SILAC, TMT/iTRAQ and targeted (SRM/PRM) quantitation.
Explain how phosphopeptides are enriched and localised to specific residues.
Describe yeast two-hybrid, affinity purification MS, proximity labelling and cross-linking MS for protein interactions.
Explain how protein and mRNA levels can disagree and why.
Describe the Human Protein Atlas and Human Proteome Project as community resources.
Outline how genomic, transcriptomic and proteomic data can be integrated, with an example.

keyConcepts.definition: Comparing peptide signal intensity or spectral counts between separate runs; flexible but sensitive to run-to-run variation.
Cells grown in media containing heavy isotope-labelled lysine and arginine are mixed with light controls before processing, giving accurate relative quantitation.
Isobaric chemical tags label peptides from several samples, which are pooled; reporter ions released in MS/MS give relative abundance (affected by ratio compression).
SRM/MRM or PRM monitors predefined peptides with high sensitivity and reproducibility for validation.
Post-translational modification such as phosphorylation, ubiquitination, acetylation or glycosylation that changes protein activity, location or stability.
Using TiO2 or immobilised metal affinity chromatography to capture low-abundance phosphopeptides before MS.
Affinity purification of a bait protein with its interaction partners followed by MS identification.
A genetic assay in which bait-prey interaction reconstitutes a transcription factor and activates a reporter gene.
Fusing an enzyme (BioID, APEX) to a bait so nearby proteins are biotinylated and later purified and identified.

deeper.beginner: Quantitative proteomics is a before-and-after photograph of the proteome: which proteins rise when a cell is stressed, treated or infected. PTM proteomics focuses on the switches. Interactomics maps who touches whom. Then integration asks whether the changes in RNA and protein agree, and where they do not, that is often where post-transcriptional regulation lives.
deeper.intermediate: SILAC gives the most accurate relative quantitation in cultured cells because samples are combined early, minimising handling variation. TMT multiplexes up to 18 samples in one run but suffers from ratio compression due to co-isolated peptides, which MS3 or ion-mobility methods reduce. Phosphoproteomics typically identifies tens of thousands of sites and uses localisation scores (for example Ascore, PTMProphet) to assign the modified residue. Y2H detects binary interactions but with many false positives and negatives; AP-MS detects complexes in near-native conditions but cannot tell direct from indirect contacts.
deeper.advanced: mRNA and protein levels correlate only moderately, with the discrepancies attributed to translation rate, protein half-life and technical noise, so protein-level evidence is needed for functional claims. Cross-linking MS gives distance restraints between residues and complements cryo-EM and AlphaFold structural models. Multi-omics integration (for example proteogenomics, which searches MS data against a sample-specific genomic database) can find variant peptides and novel coding regions. The Human Protein Atlas combines antibody-based imaging with MS and RNA data to map where each protein is expressed in tissues and cells.

commonMistakes: Assuming mRNA level predicts protein level or activity.
Treating a Y2H positive as proof of interaction in vivo without orthogonal validation.
Forgetting that phosphoproteomic changes may reflect changes in protein abundance rather than increased phosphorylation.
